An arithmetic expression shall additionally require its selected operation, component format, controls, and delivery claim. Section 12 defines the resource contract for a selected stronger operation.

The implementation shall select the operation/profile pair before evaluation:

| Selected operation | Applicable arithmetic contract |
| --- | --- |
| `component_exact` | Finite references in Section 4, zero signs in Section 5, and nonfinite dispatch in Sections 6-8. This is an explicit stronger accuracy contract. |
| `scalar_steps` with observed scalar execution | The scalar graphs in Section 11.2 for finite arithmetic, Sections 6-8 for nonfinite dispatch, and selected local-status delivery. |
| `scalar_steps` with Native scalar execution | The scalar graphs in Section 11.2 applied through the Native provider for all prepared inputs, with that provider's admitted transformations, special values, and unobserved events. |
| Explicit report/try/checked | The corresponding selected value algorithm with an observed scalar operation contract and Section 9's report aggregation. |

Ordinary Native scalar steps require no complete-operation flag collection or nonfinite repair pass. A selected `component_exact` or named observed interface shall realize its own stronger function. Representation operations retain their specified bit behavior under every arithmetic selector.

### 2. Representation and construction

For a claimed fixed-format representation, `complex<T>` shall contain two inline objects of the same scalar type `T`, in declaration order:

```text
T real;
T imag;
```

The standard layout shall place `real` at offset zero and `imag` at `sizeof(T)`, with size `2 * sizeof(T)` and alignment `alignof(T)`. Scalar padding remains scalar padding; the two scalar objects constitute the complete Complex representation.

Foreign transport shall bind both this representation and the selected calling convention through its explicit ABI descriptor.

Examples:

```cpp
complex<f64> position(3.0, 4.0);
complex<f32> coefficient(1.0, -0.0);
complex<f64> origin(0.0, 0.0);
auto product(position * position);
```

Two-component construction shall directly initialize the scalar subobjects under their selected conversion rules. Storing same-format components is a representation transfer, including for infinity and signaling NaN.

The initializers shall evaluate once in declaration order. Same-format construction and copy shall preserve both scalar encodings, including zero signs and signaling-NaN bits. The core construction and lifetime model supplies their object transitions.

One-real-argument construction shall initialize the imaginary component to positive zero. Typed default construction shall use two scalar positive-zero encodings from their representation provider.

Direct component access shall follow the core subobject lifetime, pointer, and aliasing model.

### 3. Binding, mixed operands, and conversions

#### 3.1 One component format per operation

An ordinary binary operation on `complex<A>` and `complex<B>` uses `complex<C>`, where `C` is the existing permitted scalar common type. The common type is selected from enabled formats using the complete finite-value inclusion rule, including subnormals.

Typed cross-family operands shall use their scalar family's explicit conversion rules. A missing or ambiguous common format requires an explicit conversion or destination.

A real operand from the same permitted floating family may participate through the corresponding scalar common type and a lift to `(real,+0)`. An untyped numeric literal can bind to the component format according to existing literal rules. This is one specified lift, not a second arithmetic model for real arguments.

Examples, assuming the relevant capabilities are enabled:

```cpp
complex<f32> z(1.0, 2.0);
f32 scale(2.0);
auto doubled(z * scale);
auto shifted(z + 1.0);
```

A typed integer operand shall enter the floating family through an explicit admitted conversion.

#### 3.2 Operand preparation

After source evaluation, the operation shall prepare any required format conversions in order `left.real`, `left.imag`, `right.real`, `right.imag`. Same-format preparation preserves each component's representation. Converted components use their selected scalar conversion; the ensuing algorithm consumes those prepared encodings.

An observed invocation shall include preparation events in its own operation scope and report. If preparation quiets an sNaN, subsequent selection sees the prepared qNaN while the recorded preparation event remains. Native preparation uses the provider's ordinary conversion contract with unobserved events. Argument-expression effects precede this operation-owned preparation under the core call model.

#### 3.3 Complex-to-complex conversion

Conversion to complex<U> shall apply the selected scalar conversion to real and then imaginary components. Named Checked and Exact conversions shall retain Chapter 04's acceptance predicates.

The corresponding try_checked_cast<complex<U>> and try_exact_cast<complex<U>> shall return NumericResult<complex<U>>. Both scalar projections shall complete before result selection. The result status shall union their flags and OR their Boolean event fields. If either projection fails, the error code shall come from the first failing component in real/imaginary order. Otherwise the operation shall directly construct the two-component destination. This conversion-error order is separate from arithmetic event-mask priority.

A caller requiring each component's separate failure/status shall explicitly invoke the corresponding scalar conversions on z.real and z.imag. An Exact probe shall preserve ambient status under Chapter 04. A returning failed assignment shall preserve its existing destination; prior operand effects remain complete.

#### 3.4 Complex-to-real conversion

A scalar conversion from Complex shall select an explicit interface. try_checked_cast<U> and try_exact_cast<U> shall return NumericResult<U>. They shall first inspect the imaginary representation for numerical zero, admitting either zero sign. A nonzero, infinite, or NaN imaginary component shall return Err(InvalidOperation) with empty NumericStatus while preserving the representation and ambient FP status. On zero, the operation shall apply the selected scalar conversion to the real component and return its result. The matching value interfaces use Chapter 04's delivery.

Direct z.real access selects that component independently of this whole-value conversion predicate.

### 4. Finite arithmetic and result precision

Let `z = (a,b)` and `w = (c,d)` contain finite values of the prepared scalar format. Let `Rr` and `Ri` be the real and imaginary rounding modes. By default both equal the operation's resolved scalar rounding mode; an explicit operation may supply a pair.

A selected `component_exact` operation shall use the corresponding exact mathematical reference in this table:

| Operation | Exact real component | Exact imaginary component |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `z + w` | `a + c` | `b + d` |
| `z - w` | `a - c` | `b - d` |
| `z * w` | `a*c - b*d` | `a*d + b*c` |
| `z / w`, with nonzero `w` | `(a*c + b*d)/(c*c + d*d)` | `(b*c - a*d)/(c*c + d*d)` |

Each exact output component is rounded directly into `T` once. Arithmetic internal to these definitions has no finite-format intermediate overflow, underflow, or Inexact event. The final component roundings produce the applicable flags using the established scalar rules, including tininess-after.

Exact finite division shall classify a zero divisor from c and d themselves. A nonzero subnormal divisor shall take the nonzero-divisor reference regardless of internal arithmetic choices.

Each component shall independently receive its prescribed projection and status, including Overflow for an out-of-range reference.

Examples with `M` the maximum finite scalar, `t` the minimum positive subnormal, and nearest-even rounding:

| Operation | Result | Local flags |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `(M,M)/(M,M)` | `(1,+0)` | None. |
| `(t,t)/(t,t)` | `(1,+0)` | None. |
| `(M,M)/(1,1)` | `(M,+0)` | None. |
| `(M,M)*(M,-M)` | `(+Infinity,+0)` | Overflow and Inexact for the real component only. |
| `(t,t)*(1/2,1/2)` | `(+0,t)` | None. |

The exactness boundary is one complex operator. In z*w+v the product shall project before the addition. Optimization shall preserve these selected values and observations unless the caller explicitly selects a contract admitting another graph.

A component_exact claim shall identify each supported operation, component format, control combination, and delivery form. Within that claim, the provider shall deliver the specified projections and selected status throughout the admitted input domain. Its mathematical reference shall determine the required result; the provider may select any algorithm satisfying that result and its published resource contract.

### 5. Exact signed-zero rules

An exact finite intermediate carries a mathematical value and, if that value is zero, a zero-sign bit.

1. A zero product has the XOR of the two operand sign bits.
2. Subtraction negates the second exact operand before addition, including its zero sign.
3. Exact addition of two same-sign zeros preserves that sign.
4. Any other exact sum equal to zero, including nonzero cancellation or opposite-sign zeros, is negative zero only under toward-negative rounding; it is positive zero under the other four standard modes.
5. Each result component uses its own rounding mode when applying rule 4.
6. In finite complex division, the exact denominator is strictly positive, so an exactly zero numerator retains its sign in the quotient.
7. A nonzero exact result rounded to zero uses the sign of that nonzero result. This is distinct from an exactly zero result.

These rules apply to the specified exact component formulas, including finite axis denominators. No extra division-by-one or multiplication-by-one identity rule overrides them.

For finite nonzero `z`, `z/z` is numerically `(1,0)`. Under toward-negative, its imaginary zero can be negative. Likewise, `(1,-0)*(1,+0)` has imaginary positive zero under nearest-even. Numerical identities are not blanket bit-preserving transformations.

Bitwise conjugation and copying are defined separately in Section 10. They retain their precise representation guarantees.

### 6. Classification and NaN selection

Classification reads the prepared representation without arithmetic. Each scalar is finite (including either zero), positive/negative infinity, quiet NaN, or signaling NaN.

For a complex value:

- `is_zero` means both components are numerical zero.
- `is_finite` means both components are finite.
- `has_infinity` means at least one component is infinite.
- `has_nan` means at least one component is NaN.

The last two properties can both be true. Classification shall retain each component's NaN and infinity information for the selected special-case dispatch.

The implementation shall apply Chapter 04's deterministic propagation algorithm to the ordered prepared components `(a,b,c,d)`. If an input NaN is selected, multiplication/division shall return that selected quiet NaN in both components and place signaling-input Invalid in common status. This selected branch completes the operation; other branches contribute no events. The canonical generated quiet NaN Q and payload mapping are those of Chapter 04.

Addition and subtraction shall select NaNs independently for (a,c) and (b,d). Subtraction shall select from the original operand encodings before the numeric sign negation, preserving the selected NaN sign under Chapter 04.

### 7. Multiplication with nonfinite inputs

The following ordered branches define `z*w` after component preparation:

1. Apply the global NaN selection in Section 6. If selected, return immediately.
2. If all four components are finite, use the exact finite operation in Section 4.
3. If one entire complex operand is zero and the other has an infinity, return `(Q,Q)` with operation-common Invalid.
4. Otherwise evaluate the extended products and sums defined below.

#### 7.1 Extended product convention

For each of the four terms `a*c`, `b*d`, `a*d`, and `b*c` in branch 4:

- If either factor is zero, produce exact signed zero with XOR sign, even when the other factor is infinite.
- Otherwise, if either factor is infinite, produce an infinity with XOR sign.
- Otherwise produce the exact finite product, without rounding into `T`.

This zero-term convention belongs only to branch 4 of the complex operation. It does not change scalar `0*Infinity`, and it does not bypass the entire-zero-operand rejection in branch 3.

Compute the real difference and imaginary sum from these extended terms:

- Opposite-sign infinities in an addition produce `Q` and Invalid for that result component.
- Same-sign infinities, or an infinity combined with a finite term, produce the indicated infinity without a new range event.
- Finite exact sums use Section 5 zero signs and one final rounding into `T`.

NaN generated in one result component does not cause a second global input-NaN propagation pass over the other output.

#### 7.2 Consequences

| Inputs | Result under nearest-even | Local flags |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `(Infinity,2)*(1,+0)` | `(Infinity,2)` | None. |
| `(Infinity,2)*(+0,1)` | `(-2,Infinity)` | None. |
| `(+0,+0)*(Infinity,2)` | `(Q,Q)` | Invalid. |
| `(Infinity,+0)*(+0,Infinity)` | `(+0,Infinity)` | None. |
| `(Infinity,Infinity)*(1,1)` | `(Q,Infinity)` | Real Invalid. |
| `(Infinity,Infinity)*(1,-1)` | `(Infinity,Q)` | Imaginary Invalid. |

The first two cases explain why a blanket replacement of every finite companion component by zero is not a suitable default: it loses known values. Conversely, an indeterminate infinity cancellation is not converted into a claimed exact finite zero.

### 8. Division: complete ordered dispatch

Let prepared inputs be `(a,b)` and `(c,d)`. Evaluate the branches in the order written; the first matching branch determines the result. Helper calculations that are described as exact do not expose intermediate FP flags.

#### D1. Input NaN

Apply Section 6 global NaN selection and return if it selects a NaN.

#### D2. All finite, nonzero divisor

If all four components are finite and `(c,d)` is not complex zero, use the exact finite quotient. This branch includes all finite real-axis and imaginary-axis denominators, so their zero signs follow the uniform finite formulas.

#### D3. Complex-zero divisor

If `c` and `d` are both numerical zero:

- If `a` and `b` are also both zero, return `(Q,Q)` with common Invalid.
- Otherwise treat `c` as the selected directed real-axis zero. For each numerator component `x`, XOR its sign with the sign of `c`:

| Numerator component `x` | Result component | Component flag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Either signed zero | The resulting signed zero | None. |
| Finite nonzero | Infinity with the resulting sign | DivideByZero. |
| Either infinity | Infinity with the resulting sign | None. |

The sign of the imaginary divisor zero `d` is not used in this branch. This is an explicit CPN26 convention for a singular complex operation, not an inference about an unspecified path by which a complex value approached zero.

Preserving a zero numerator component here does not redefine scalar `0/0`. Entire complex `0/0` has already selected Invalid.

An infinite numerator with a finite nonzero companion can still generate a component DivideByZero event for that companion. For example, `(Infinity,2)/(+0,+0)` produces `(Infinity,Infinity)` and an imaginary DivideByZero event.

#### D4. Real-axis divisor on the nonfinite path

If `d` is zero and `c` is nonzero, return the scalar operations `(a/c,b/c)` with real and imaginary result rounding respectively. Scalar division handles infinity and zero using its established rules.

This preserves independently known components, for example `(Infinity,2)/(1,+0) = (Infinity,2)`.

#### D5. Imaginary-axis divisor on the nonfinite path

If `c` is zero and `d` is nonzero, return the scalar operations `(b/d,(-a)/d)`.

The negation of `a` precedes division and its rounding. Computing `a/d`, rounding it, and negating afterward is not generally equivalent under directed rounding.

#### D6. Finite numerator, infinite non-axis divisor

If the numerator is finite and the divisor has an infinity, construct two exact direction components:

```text
C = signed 1 if c is infinite; otherwise signed zero with c's sign
D = signed 1 if d is infinite; otherwise signed zero with d's sign

c0 = c if c is finite; otherwise signed zero with c's sign
d0 = d if d is finite; otherwise signed zero with d's sign
```

Compute exact leading and residual terms using the respective result's zero-sign rounding mode:

```text
leading_real = a*C + b*D
leading_imag = b*C - a*D
residual_real = a*c0 + b*d0
residual_imag = b*c0 - a*d0
```

Both output components are zeros. Determine each sign as follows:

1. If its leading term is nonzero, use that sign.
2. Otherwise, if its residual term is nonzero, use the residual sign.
3. Otherwise, use the leading term's exact zero sign from Section 5.

This branch raises no new Underflow or Inexact: the zeros come from the chosen infinity extension, not finite-format rounding of a small nonzero quotient.

Using unit coefficients for infinite inputs is a zero-sign convention. It does not assert that two stored infinities reveal the magnitudes or growth rates of their pre-overflow sources.

The residual matters: `(0,-1)/(Infinity,2)` returns `(-0,-0)`, while a direction-only calculation could lose the real zero's sign. Likewise, `(1,+0)/(Infinity,1)` returns `(+0,-0)`.

#### D7. Infinity in both numerator and divisor, remaining non-axis cases

Return `(Q,Q)` with common Invalid. Equal infinity encodings are not evidence that the original magnitudes were equal; this branch does not simplify an infinity-containing self-division to one.

Axis branches have already taken precedence. For example, `(Infinity,2)/(Infinity,+0)` returns `(Q,+0)` with real Invalid through D4, preserving its known imaginary result.

#### D8. Infinite numerator, finite non-axis divisor

At this point the numerator has an infinity and `c,d` are finite and both nonzero. Let `A,B` map infinite numerator components to signed one and finite numerator components to signed zero. Compute:

```text
u = A*c + B*d
v = B*c - A*d
```

For each result component:

- A nonzero exact direction yields an infinity with that sign.
- A zero direction yields `Q` and component Invalid.

Here a cancellation between infinite contributions does not establish an exact zero. For example, `(Infinity,Infinity)/(1,1)` yields `(Infinity,Q)` with imaginary Invalid.

#### 8.1 Exhaustiveness

After D1 removes NaN cases, each component is finite or infinite. D2 handles every finite/nonzero quotient; D3 handles every remaining zero divisor; D4/D5 handle axes. In the remaining non-axis domain, either only the denominator is infinite (D6), both operands have infinity (D7), or only the numerator is infinite (D8). No residual case has undefined arithmetic behavior.

The component encoding of any returned NaN is specified by the selected input payload or by canonical `Q`. Flags are defined by the selected branch and final scalar roundings, not by incidental instructions used to implement the branch.

### 9. Observed Complex reports

A selected observed Complex operation shall determine its value and local preparation, real/imaginary, and operation-common events. The public NumericStatus shall combine their Boolean fields by OR and their flags by union:

```text
operation_flags = preparation_flags union real_flags
                  union imag_flags union common_flags
```

Common status records whole-operation conditions such as the global signaling-input rule or complex zero/zero. Each component status records that component's projection/events. The semantic calculation shall attribute each event to its source stage. A function exposing detailed component reports shall use its declared public report type; the ordinary NumericStatus exposes the aggregate.

The completed report shall use [Chapter 04](#chapter-04-numeric-integration)'s delivery algorithm. `require_finite` succeeds precisely when both components are finite. A report retains each computed component, while a failed NumericResult contains no readable complex value. A returning checked mutation commits the whole selected value after successful classification; this commit is an object update rather than a concurrent two-word atomic store.

Ordinary Native scalar-step execution delivers its provider result without establishing this report. Explicitly requesting a report/try/checked operation selects local observation and its necessary support. Preparation and component calculations shall finish under the selected nontrapping observation scope before that stronger interface selects delivery.

### 10. Equality, ordering, and representation operations

#### 10.1 Numeric equality

After permitted type binding, equality shall return true when both component numeric comparisons are true. An observed comparison uses quiet scalar equality: either zero sign compares equal, qNaN compares false, and each sNaN comparison contributes Invalid even when another component already decides the Boolean result. A Native comparison uses its provider's admitted comparison graph and unobserved events.

`z != w` is the logical negation of this completed equality operation. It does not perform a second comparison with different status. Numeric equality is not an identity test for an object containing a NaN.

#### 10.2 Explicit ordering and representation equality

Ordered use of Complex shall select an explicit comparator. Numeric equality and the following named representation ordering shall use their separately admitted operation claims.

`total_order_lex` and `representation_equal` require identical component formats and compatible representation contracts. They do not perform the arithmetic operand preparation of Section 3.2 or any implicit common-format conversion. A caller requiring a cross-format comparison shall explicitly convert the operands first; any resulting conversion status belongs to that explicit conversion.

The standard named `total_order_lex` compares real components by the component provider's non-arithmetic total order and, if equal in that order, compares imaginary components the same way. It neither quiets sNaNs nor raises Invalid. Its lexicographic ordering is a container/sorting contract, not a claim that complex numbers possess a compatible real-number ordering.

`representation_equal` compares the two meaningful scalar encodings, including zero signs and NaN class/sign/payload. It excludes unrelated object padding. Whole-object `memcmp` is not substituted as a portable definition when a component representation contains padding or noncanonical encodings. Such encodings follow the selected component provider's declared representation contract.

#### 10.3 Copy, unary signs, and conjugation

Same-format copy and unary plus preserve both component representations. Unary minus flips each component's sign field. Conjugation copies the real component and flips only the imaginary sign field. These representation transformations:

- preserve NaN payloads and signaling/quiet class;
- do not generate FP flags;
- preserve or change zero signs exactly as specified;
- do not pass through arithmetic addition, multiplication, or conversion.

Thus applying conjugation twice restores both original component encodings, including an sNaN. Replacing conjugation by a general complex multiplication would not meet this contract.

Mathematical simplifications involving arithmetic still need proof about NaNs, zero signs, rounding, and flags. For example, the existence of a representation-preserving unary plus does not make adding an arbitrary signed-zero complex operand a universal bitwise identity.

### 11. Configurable arithmetic profiles and providers

#### 11.1 Exact and ordinary selection

The sole preset table in Chapter 08 selects ordinary Complex/scalar execution. That default shall become an arithmetic capability requirement at the operation's use. A component_exact use shall explicitly select the value and special-case references in Sections 4-8. A Native scalar_steps use shall select the following graph and its Native provider permissions. Function definitions shall retain the operation/profile contract they publish across imports and optimization.

#### 11.2 Explicit scalar-step arithmetic

The scalar_steps profile shall instantiate this scalar-operation graph for prepared z=(a,b) and w=(c,d):

| Complex operation | Real graph | Imaginary graph |
| --- | --- | --- |
| z+w | add(a,c) | add(b,d) |
| z-w | sub(a,c) | sub(b,d) |
| z*w | sub(mul(a,c),mul(b,d)) | add(mul(a,d),mul(b,c)) |
| z/w | div(add(mul(a,c),mul(b,d)),add(mul(c,c),mul(d,d))) | div(sub(mul(b,c),mul(a,d)),add(mul(c,c),mul(d,d))) |

With observed scalar execution, finite nodes shall project to T under their component's selected rounding mode. The invocation shall sequence the real graph before the imaginary graph and collect each component's node events before Section 9 delivery. It may share a node when both value and observed event semantics agree. Nonfinite inputs and an actual complex-zero divisor shall instead use Sections 6-8.

With Native scalar execution, the graph shall apply to every prepared input, including nonfinite values and complex zero divisors. Every node shall use its Native provider operation and environment. The compiler may share, contract, reassociate, or otherwise transform nodes within that provider's declared permissions. The invocation shall deliver the target result/fault directly with unobserved arithmetic events.

A denominator rounded to zero within the graph shall use its scalar division behavior. Observed intermediate Overflow, Underflow, Invalid, and Inexact belong to this graph; component_exact uses its separate final-projection reference.

#### 11.3 Provider and control binding

A provider shall publish its supported operation/profile, component-format, control, and delivery combinations, together with their permitted value/error behavior, special values, observation capability, and resources. A claim for one combination shall bind exactly its stated dependencies. Custom approximations and Native transformations shall use their published contracts. Finite-input assumptions shall require explicit selection. The compiler shall realize a requested claim or diagnose its absence at that use.

Explicit component rounding or stronger accuracy requirements shall bind their requested capability. Ordinary Native execution has no obligatory software fallback. The bound numerical contract shall identify the relevant operation profile independently from the two-component storage layout.

### 12. Selected resources and decimal representation

#### 12.1 Resource binding

Each arithmetic claim shall publish its resource requirements together with its operation, format, controls, and delivery contract. The descriptor shall identify fixed internal storage requirements, any explicitly supplied temporary workspace or resource domain, and the resource-failure outlet. An allocation-free claim shall realize the selected result within its published fixed-storage contract. An allocating claim shall acquire and release temporary storage through its named resource domain under the ordinary numeric resource rules.

A source form with explicit resource arguments shall bind those arguments. An ordinary operator or another source form with no resource argument shall bind either an allocation-free implementation or an explicitly configured resource domain admitted by that claim. Binding shall establish this choice before operand evaluation. Its effect signature and support dependencies shall expose the selected resource behavior.

Returning resource failure shall preserve the destination and retire temporary resources under the selected numeric failure contract. A value interface shall use its stated terminal outlet where that contract selects termination. Successful execution shall deliver the selected mathematical result and status. The provider may choose native primitives, scaling, staged computation, or multiprecision work consistent with this observable contract.

The exact formulas in Section 4 shall define mathematical references. They shall leave intermediate representation and workspace organization to the bound provider. Format support, Complex storage, and scalar-step execution shall retain their independently selected resource requirements.

#### 12.2 Decimal component formats

The finite component equations and classification rules apply to enabled decimal floating formats as well, using their scalar rounding and flag contracts. Correct numerical values do not alone select a unique decimal cohort or byte encoding.

The selected scalar decimal provider shall declare a deterministic canonical round-from-exact/cohort rule for newly computed components, including zero exponent selection, and bind it to the profile's representation fingerprint. A Complex operation shall use that declared rule to select the computed representation.

Same-format copying and conjugation shall preserve their specified meaningful bits. A computed component shall use its selected decimal arithmetic provider's declared result/cohort rule.

### 13. Constant evaluation and diagnostics

Complex constant evaluation shall use the selected target operation/profile pair and the canonical numeric rules in Chapter 04. Runtime optimization shall preserve the selected observations or remain within its Native provider permissions. The compiler shall apply Chapter 04's numeric applicability cases and Chapter 08's severity policy. This chapter supplies no separate severity or event-priority table.

### 14. SIMD and GPU delta

A Complex vector lane comprises one real/imaginary pair. Its mask selects that whole pair. Chapter 04's vector contract defines inactive representations, observed active-lane aggregation, Native speculative arithmetic permissions, and reduction behavior. A placement provider shall declare any structure-of-arrays or other transport mapping in addition to the scalar Complex object representation.

### 15. Selected conformance

A provider shall satisfy each operation/profile, format, control, and delivery combination it advertises, together with that combination's declared dependencies and resources. A representation claim shall provide the two-component layout and its selected construction/transfers. A component_exact claim shall satisfy the applicable finite and exceptional references above. A Native claim shall satisfy its versioned operation and transformation descriptor. Foreign transport shall follow the native interoperability contract independently of numerical accuracy.

---

<a id="chapter-06-construction-execution"></a>

## CPN26 Construction and Destruction Execution Specification

### 1. Scope and Required Distinctions

This chapter owns object and subobject state, construction planning, delegation, destruction responsibility, Whole, Cleanup, Abandon, and storage reuse. Implementations shall apply these transitions within the [abstract machine](#chapter-21-abstract-machine-conformance). Configuration and validation defaults belong to [Chapter 08](#chapter-08-runtime-configuration); failure outlets and continuation belong to [Chapter 28](#chapter-28-error-recovery).

Each object lifetime shall identify its storage extent and destruction responsibility separately. Lifetime termination consumes the selected destruction obligation; storage release consumes the separate storage-ownership capability. Responsibility transfer preserves object location and storage ownership. Reconstruction shall establish a new generation, including at the same address and with the same type.

For inheritance and Whole, the complete-object boundary shall be the most-derived class lifetime containing the selected base. Each class-valued member or array element shall have its own inheritance boundary. Whole shall affect that boundary and its associated destruction continuations.

The cleanup algorithms below shall execute on the continuing paths admitted by the selected failure outlet. A terminal outlet shall end execution at its defined boundary. Native numerical operations use their selected native fault/result contract; named checked operations retain their specified failure outlet.

### 2. Declaration and Lifecycle Grammar

The [consolidated grammar](#chapter-15-grammar-binding) is authoritative for lifecycle source forms. This chapter assigns the following operations their meaning:

| Source form | Semantic role |
| --- | --- |
| `T object(arguments) -> { ... };` | Ordinary construction plus a construction tail in one transaction. |
| `init member(arguments);` | Explicit initialization producer. Base and virtual-base selectors identify their corresponding slots. |
| `delegate(arguments);` | Invoke the selected constructor activation at this statement. |
| `~T() { ... } cleanup { ... }` | Destructor body followed by the layer's Cleanup phase. |
| `Complete member;`, `Complete base<B>;`, `Complete virtual_base<V>;`, `Complete;` | Select the local destruction responsibilities in Section 7. |
| `destruction_owner<V> = base_path<...>;` | Bind the unique virtual-base obligation to a nominated class layer. |

`class Manual T` shall select the local-member policy in Section 7. Complete and owner declarations shall appear in the class body. A destructor shall have one zero-parameter declaration with the dedicated return-type-free syntax. Its noexcept contract shall cover its body, Cleanup, and generated obligations. Virtual properties and other function modifiers shall follow Chapter 10.

`base_path<Left, B>` shall identify successive direct-base edges from the operation's statically typed view, or from the declaring layer for an Owner declaration. Each edge shall exist and the final entry shall identify the selected subobject. A type-only selector shall require a unique reachable match. Initialization and takeover selectors shall retain their direct-base or virtual-base scope. The compile-time path shall disambiguate requests such as `destroy_base<base_path<Left, B>>(object)` and corresponding Owner bindings.

Object declarations, function declarations, const qualification, and constexpr requirements shall use Chapter 10 and Chapter 15. In an ordinary declaration context, the parser shall classify `T name(...);` as an object declaration and diagnose its initializer under that classification. An external-linkage declaration context shall use Chapter 15's dedicated function, external-object declaration, and define-object productions; a define-object shall use this chapter's initialization transaction.

An omitted or empty argument list shall select typed default initialization. Basic types shall receive their defined zero value; a class shall invoke viable default construction. A type lacking that operation shall require an explicit initializer. The selected type contract shall determine its representation.

Construction shall initialize a const object through its construction permissions. After the relevant subobject becomes initialized, mutation shall require its ordinary qualification contract. Destruction and authorized storage operations shall use their independent lifetime and ownership permissions.

```text
i32 count(10);
auto copy(count);
const i32 limit(64);
constexpr i32 capacity(256);
Widget item(args) -> {
    init cache(cache_args);
    inspect_initialized_members(this);
};
```

A construction tail shall contribute initialization declarations to the same transaction and execute its ordinary statements after the selected constructor and delegation chain return. The object shall become Alive after the tail completes. An omitted constructor argument list shall select default construction. The transaction shall construct directly in final storage.

A class shall have viable generated default and aggregate candidates. The aggregate shall initialize direct nonstatic members in declaration order and default-construct bases. A user constructor with the same signature shall replace that candidate; other generated candidates shall retain their individual viability requirements. A missing default for a required base or omitted member shall make that candidate unavailable.

### 3. Object State and Canonical Order

A complete-object transaction shall have Constructing, Alive, Destroying, Destroyed, or Abandoned state. Destructor Body and Cleanup shall be subphases of Destroying. Whole shall be the irreversible control condition defined in Section 9.

Each immediate subobject slot records, logically, one of Pending, Constructing, Alive, Destroying, Destroyed, or Abandoned. A slot also identifies its current lifetime generation and destruction strategy. These are semantic distinctions. The implementation shall represent each distinction only to the extent required by selected execution and validation contracts, using control flow, activation data, or an admitted storage registration.

Canonical construction order is:

1. Distinct virtual bases of the most-derived object, in dependency-respecting depth-first order, following base declarations left to right and emitting a virtual base after its own base dependencies; emit each virtual-base identity once.
2. Direct nonvirtual bases in declaration order.
3. Direct nonstatic data members in declaration order.

Each base or member shall complete its recursive construction before the next sibling slot begins. Arrays shall construct in increasing index order. Each class layer shall execute its own hierarchical plan.

The most-derived layer shall supply effective virtual-base initialization declarations. When a constructor is invoked for a base subobject, its virtual-base declarations shall be checked for declaration validity and remain dormant. Evaluation shall visit only producers selected by the effective plan.

The canonical destruction order shall reverse successful construction within this hierarchy. Shared virtual bases shall form one complete-object tail in reverse virtual-base construction order. Intermediate base destruction shall leave that tail to the complete-object coordinator. Explicit early base destruction selects the Whole transition in Section 9.

The following table identifies functional information, independently of optional diagnostic tracking:

| Selected operation | Information required for its result |
| --- | --- |
| Statically determined construction/destruction | Ordered operations, representable entirely by control flow. |
| Catchable partial-construction failure | Successfully completed subobjects or array prefix. |
| Path-dependent first construction or assignment | The selected slot's Pending/Alive distinction. |
| Manual destruction, Whole, and Cleanup | Consumed obligations, continuation, and reverse frontier. |
| Dynamic virtual-base responsibility transfer | The unique current Owner binding. |
| Registered storage reconstruction | Current generation, actual type, and destruction entry. |

An implementation shall preserve this information where the selected functionality observes it. Optional raw-access validation shall follow `memory.raw_validation`; Release's contract mode relies on admitted programmer obligations and omits additional validation metadata. Explicit checked operations shall retain their specified checks. The native ABI determines which activation, sidecar, or storage representation can carry functional state.

### 4. Unified Construction Plan

#### 4.1 Plan formation

The compiler shall form one plan for the current construction layer from the selected constructor, statically resolved delegation chain, and construction tail. Each slot shall receive the first applicable producer in this precedence order:

- An explicit `init` declaration.
- Otherwise, an in-class member initializer, if present.
- Otherwise, a source-bound reservation for an ordinary first-assignment operation under the rule below.
- Otherwise, type-directed default construction.

An explicit constructor producer shall override a fallback member or typed default. Every slot shall have at most one effective explicit constructor producer. An ordinary write to a slot with an in-class or explicit initializer shall execute as assignment after that initializer; an eligible uninitialized slot shall use the reservation rule below.

A first-assignment reservation shall require first-write-before-read on every normal completion path in the constructor's source control-flow graph, using explicit `initializes` contracts and bound construction summaries that express declared source contracts. Only this declared interface evidence shall select a producer; additionally inferred implementation summaries shall serve diagnostics and optimization. Required compile-time branch selection applies before this fixed analysis. At a control-flow join, a definite first-write fact holds only when every incoming normal path establishes it. Mutually exclusive first writes share a reservation; successive writes construct and then assign.

When this source-bound rule supplies no reservation, the type-directed default remains the producer. An explicit `initializes` contract shall require the stated entry/exit transition and frontier order. Optional interprocedural analysis may refine diagnostics and code generation; the selected producer, constructor calls, and source effects shall remain those of the bound plan under every analysis mode.

An init declaration shall contribute a declarative producer from the top level of a constructor or construction tail, where it may be interleaved with ordinary statements. Its initializer expression may compute a conditional value. Runtime-dependent control flow shall express construction through eligible ordinary first assignment and its required source-bound state facts.

The declarative initializer environment shall contain constructor parameters, accessible earlier initialized subobjects, static objects, and eligible enclosing lexical bindings. Every referenced lifetime shall cover actual evaluation. Constructor-body and tail-body locals shall instead participate through ordinary statements and frontier-valid first assignment.

A deferred expression shall read its bound environment at its actual evaluation point. Earlier modifications and aliasing effects participate in that value. Each binding shall remain alive through evaluation. Substitution and code motion shall satisfy the core transformation rules for the selected execution contract.

#### 4.2 Activation and the initialization frontier

Each constructor invocation has an activation. Its parameter initialization occurs at the actual invocation point. Its explicit producers become available after those parameters exist. A construction tail's declarative environment is available when the object declaration starts its construction transaction, although its ordinary body runs later.

The initialization frontier shall be the first Pending slot in canonical order. Execution shall proceed as follows:

1. Enter the activation and make its declarative producers available.
2. At the frontier, require an available producer and initialized required inputs; evaluate its arguments once, then construct directly in the slot.
3. On success, mark that slot Alive and advance to the next Pending slot.
4. Pause frontier processing at an unavailable activation, first-assignment reservation, or unmet input-state requirement.
5. Execute ordinary statements in source order; resume the frontier after successful first construction or delegated activation entry.
6. Before returning an activation, complete every deferred producer using that activation's parameters.
7. Before committing ordinary construction and its optional tail, establish Alive for every required slot.

A typed-default producer shall be available under its plan; a delegated producer shall become available upon entry to its activation. A plan shall establish a feasible order, live deferred environments, and complete normal paths. Static readiness cycles and violations of those requirements shall fail plan validation.

#### 4.3 Delegation

`delegate(arguments);` shall evaluate its arguments once at that statement and invoke the selected overload of the same class using the existing destination and shared plan. The callee's ordinary statements shall complete before execution continues after the delegate statement.

Each activation may contain one direct delegation statement at any unconditional statement position, including an unconditional nested block. The selected chain shall be statically identifiable and acyclic. A surrounding handler may observe and rethrow failure; successful construction shall require successful completion of each reached selected delegation. If a preceding statement exits through failure, subsequent delegation shall remain unexecuted. Runtime-conditional or loop-controlled delegation shall fail this structural requirement.

The caller prelude shall execute before the source-position delegate call. A callee may return with an unrelated caller reservation still Pending when every callee-dependent producer has completed and the callee's accesses satisfy their contracts.

```text
class Example {
    i32 first;
    i32 second;

    Example(i32 x) {
        init second(mark_second(x));
        note();
        delegate(x, 0);
        after_delegate();
    }
    Example(i32 x, i32 tag) {
        init first(mark_first(x));
        inside_delegate();
    }
};
```

The required call order shall be `note`, `mark_first`, `mark_second`, `inside_delegate`, `after_delegate`, following the source-position delegation and canonical frontier.

### 5. First Assignment and Initialization-State Permissions

An ordinary construction-time assignment shall evaluate its destination under the assignment sequencing rule, then dispatch by its state:

| Destination state | Operation |
| --- | --- |
| Alive with the declared type | Execute ordinary assignment. |
| Pending with a first-assignment reservation at the frontier | Evaluate the right-hand side once and construct directly in the slot. |
| Any other state or a Pending slot beyond the frontier | Fail the required state/frontier check. |

Direct construction shall use Chapter 10's prvalue, lvalue-copy, xvalue-move, and explicit-conversion requirements. Ordinary statements shall retain source order.

An initialized assignment shall use its selected assignment operator's failure guarantee. First construction shall publish Alive only after success. Direct construction shall preserve the selected constructor and expression effects.

```text
class Pair {
    i32 first;
    i32 second;
    Pair(i32 x) {
        this->second = compute_second(x);
        this->first = compute_first(x);
    }
};
```

The first assignment is an order error because the first slot is still reserved. A valid declarative rewrite is:

```text
Pair(i32 x) {
    init second(compute_second(x));
    this->first = compute_first(x);
}
```

In the valid rewrite, the assignment shall construct the first slot, then frontier processing shall execute the deferred second producer. A body local may supply the ordinary assignment under its lexical lifetime; declarative producers shall use only Section 4.1's initializer environment.

Address formation, storage metadata, and forwarding a construction-aware view shall preserve the current object state. Reading, member invocation, copying, or value assignment shall require the expected live generation. The this pointer shall carry these same access obligations.

Initialization analysis shall use the resolved `construction.analysis` mode. Local analysis shall examine the current definition's CFG and bound declaration/interface summaries. Interprocedural analysis may additionally inspect available callee definitions. Release defaults to local analysis under Chapter 08; neither mode requires whole-program proof.

Definitions shall satisfy their read, write, initialization, escape, and lifecycle-control contracts. `[[requires_initialized(a, b), initializes(c)]]` publishes construction-state requirements: the named initialized inputs shall be Alive on entry, and each initializes slot shall be Pending on entry and Alive on normal return, respecting the frontier. An opaque call with an open access summary shall require every potentially accessed slot to be Alive. Callers may supply more precise bound contracts. Analysis mode shall preserve the source-bound producer rule in Section 4.

A proved invalid transition shall receive the central mandatory diagnostic. An admitted but unproved ordinary access or caller obligation shall retain its ANOMALY disposition and programmer responsibility. Selected checked views and validation modes shall validate the state before the governed action; contract mode shall retain the source obligation without adding a validation registry. The implementation shall still retain the functional state that selects construction, assignment, ownership, or cleanup. Explicit proof requirements and unavailable type operations retain their acceptance rules.

A selected lifecycle check shall reject before the invalid action and deliver `LifecycleError` through its declared language-failure outlet. Its coverage is the valid object/slot descriptor supplied to that check. Raw and foreign accesses retain their declared access obligations.

### 6. Construction Completion and Rollback

The most-derived object shall commit Alive after its required slots and ordinary constructor bodies, followed by the optional construction tail, complete successfully.

On a permitted construction unwind, the transaction shall destroy completed subobjects in reverse completion order. A failing subobject shall first perform its own partial rollback. An array shall roll back its completed prefix in descending index order. Pending and unsuccessfully Constructing slots shall remain outside completed-object destruction, including the incomplete complete object's ordinary destructor body.

Construction rollback shall discharge established responsibilities for completed subobjects under every Manual, Complete, and Owner policy. Constructor parameters and ordinary locals shall follow their scope-exit contracts. External side effects shall retain their operation-specific postconditions.

Cleanup failure shall follow the failure-outlet table in Chapter 28. A continuing aggregate path shall retain the primary identity, append applicable secondary records, and continue its prescribed attempts.

### 7. Destructors and Responsibility Policies

A class lacking a destructor declaration shall receive an empty-body destructor with generated subobject cleanup. Its availability shall require viable accessible selected cleanup. A user declaration shall supply the body while retaining the specified generated lifetime operations.

`virtual ~T()` shall introduce virtual destruction. Derived destructors, including implicit declarations, shall retain inherited virtual destruction. Other virtual members shall leave the destructor's independently declared status unchanged. Complete derived destruction through a base view shall require virtual destruction or an exact-complete-type checked operation.

Virtual calls during construction or destruction shall dispatch within the active class layer. Same-class delegation shall retain that layer. Each call shall satisfy its receiver-state requirements. Whole shall terminate the affected continuation; calls admitted on remaining independently live subobjects shall use their own active layers.

Local takeover rules are:

| Declaration | Selected local responsibility |
|---|---|
| `Complete member;` | Explicit handling of that direct member before the Cleanup remainder fallback. |
| `Complete base<B>;` | Explicit handling of that direct nonvirtual base subobject. |
| `Complete virtual_base<V>;` | Manual handling of the unique V obligation assigned to this layer. |
| `Complete;` | All direct members and direct nonvirtual bases of this layer. |
| `class Manual T` | All direct members of T; base policies remain separately specified. |

Each takeover shall affect only the named class layer's local obligations. A virtual base shall require its unique Owner binding and, for manual handling, its explicit takeover selection. Base internals shall retain the base layer's own policy.

An ordinary destructor body may destroy or abandon an eligible local slot, or leave a manual slot for Cleanup. Each destruction attempt shall consume its generation's obligation once, including an attempt ending in a continuing exception. A destruction entry shall require an eligible live target; reentry into a Destroying target shall fail that requirement.

### 8. Legal Owners and Virtual-Base Transfer

A legal Owner shall be a compiler-recognized class layer within the same complete object, containing the designated virtual base in its inheritance graph and distinct from that base itself.

After a virtual base completes construction, the most-derived layer shall initially own its obligation. A declaration such as `destruction_owner<Root> = Left;` shall nominate one unambiguous base path and establish its binding when both the obligation and target layer are available. The initial binding shall remain until that point. Competing bindings shall fail validation. Each established binding shall remain until consumed or changed by a permitted explicit transfer.

`transfer_destruction<Root>(left);` shall validate complete-object identity, virtual-base identity, unique current ownership, target eligibility, and lifecycle phase, then commit the new Owner binding. Failure shall retain the original binding and produce the ExceptionAggregate failure record under Chapter 28. Its Result form shall return the same failure record as a value.

Transfer shall require the complete object to be Constructing with an established obligation, or Alive. The virtual base shall be Alive, and the target layer shall have an established Owner record in an eligible Constructing or Alive state. Destruction entry shall freeze transfer eligibility.

Destruction entry shall freeze Owner bindings. The coordinator may retain an existing Owner record after that layer's body ends solely to discharge its obligation. User access shall continue to require a live generation. Virtual bases shall retire in the complete-object tail unless their legal manual Owner requests an early Whole transition. Each obligation shall retain one claim and one consumption.

### 9. Destruction Execution, Whole, and Cleanup

#### 9.1 Destruction coordinator

`destroy(object);` shall request destruction of the current object generation. Automatic scope exit shall invoke that operation for its registered live generation, then perform the separate storage action required by its owner. Explicit base-only requests shall use either equivalent form:

```text
destroy_base<Base>(this);
this->Base::~Base();
```

Both forms shall select the base subobject directly and require an unambiguous path and the corresponding destruction responsibility. Their source location shall determine ordinary-body or Cleanup timing. A scheduled automatic base call shall use the coordinator rule below.

The coordinator shall enter Destroying, freeze responsibility bindings, and retain one consumption record per subobject. Its reverse frontier shall be the next unresolved slot in canonical destruction order, skipping ended generations.

For each class layer, the coordinator shall:

1. Enter its ordinary destructor body when Whole has left that containing layer eligible for body entry.
2. On normal completion or a permitted continuing exception, destroy the automatic reverse-frontier prefix up to the first unresolved manual slot.
3. Execute its Cleanup body once, treating an absent body as empty.
4. Sweep all remaining local slots in reverse order, including manual remainders.
5. Leave unconsumed shared virtual-base obligations for the complete-object tail.

Cleanup shall observe the completed prefix as ended and the blocked remainder in its current states. This ordering shall preserve the reverse order across a manual barrier.

An explicit member-destruction request inside Cleanup shall designate its reverse-frontier slot. A proved out-of-order request is invalid; an unknown obligation follows the selected analysis/validation policy. The final reverse sweep shall consume slots left untouched by Cleanup. Ordinary destructor-body manual requests use their separate source-position rule.

#### 9.2 Whole control effect

A permitted source-initiated base-only destruction or Abandon request shall latch Whole for the containing inheritance boundary, then perform the selected attempt. This rule includes a request at Cleanup's current frontier. A base invocation generated by the coordinator shall remain scheduled destruction. All other slots shall retain their consumption records.

After the early attempt, control shall exit the affected ordinary body or Cleanup and continue through the coordinator's required Cleanup and reverse-remainder work. An entered Cleanup shall retain its consumed invocation state. Whole shall use the lifecycle control channel, separate from user exception handlers and process termination.

Whole shall propagate through CPN26 helpers executing the affected destructor or Cleanup continuation, causing their generated exits. Its callable contract shall expose the required lifecycle effect through declarations, inferred internal summaries, and indirect function types. Lowering shall use control-flow edges or equivalent internal status while preserving the selected exit work.

An affected body or helper exit shall perform its required local-object and temporary cleanup. Each cleanup failure shall follow Chapter 28's selected outlet, which determines continuation or termination.

An early base request on an Alive complete object shall begin Destroying and Whole together. Containing layers requiring the ended base shall proceed directly to their eligible Cleanup and remainder work. Other live subobjects shall execute their own body/Cleanup sequences. Upon completion, an ordinary external caller shall resume through the operation's return or failure contract. A Constructing object shall use construction rollback; early base requests in that state shall fail lifecycle validation.

The selected base attempt shall deliver its failure before the Whole continuation proceeds. Chapter 28 shall determine aggregation on a continuing path or immediate Release destructor termination.

#### 9.3 Cleanup access and failure

Cleanup shall resolve names for automatic, manual, base, virtual-base, destroyed, and abandoned slots under the class's ordinary access rights. Dead slots admit storage/state inspection; typed value operations require a live generation. Remaining live slots retain the current class layer's ordinary typed-operation contracts.

Cleanup shall use destruction and permitted inspection for its local obligations. Abandon eligibility shall be exactly Section 10.1's preconditions. A Cleanup exception shall finish that invocation and pass its record to the selected continuing aggregate path, whose coordinator shall perform remaining reverse work. Control-flow and functional state shall represent that continuation under Section 3.

### 10. Abandon, Arrays, and Storage Reuse

#### 10.1 Abandon scope

`abandon(object);` shall end the selected Alive object and recursively its live contained lifetimes, including its virtual bases and member/element lifetimes. It shall consume their destruction obligations through the Abandon transition and preserve storage ownership, storage bytes, and external resource postconditions. Destructors and Cleanup belong to the distinct destruction operation.

Complete-object Abandon shall require Alive before destruction entry. Member Abandon shall require an Alive member and an eligible ordinary-code or destructor-body context. Cleanup and construction rollback shall use their specified cleanup operations. The containing object's other members shall retain their states, and later typed operations shall respect the ended member.

`abandon_base<Base>(object);` shall validate the selected direct or virtual base and its destruction responsibility, abandon its nonvirtual containment subtree, consume its obligation, and initiate Whole for that inheritance boundary. It shall require an Alive selected base and an eligible ordinary-code or destructor-body context. The resulting exit and external-return behavior shall follow Section 9.2.

Abandon of a nonvirtual layer shall preserve separately shared virtual-base obligations. If that layer owns a still-live virtual base, the coordinator shall retain its existing frozen claim until consumption. An explicit Abandon of that virtual base or its complete object shall consume the corresponding claim. Every shared virtual base shall therefore have one resolved obligation.

`abandon(array);` shall end the array and its live elements. `abandon(array[index]);` shall evaluate its index once under ordinary bounds rules and end only that element. Array destruction shall visit remaining live generations once in descending index order.

Abandon shall use Chapter 08's ANOMALY disposition. Diagnostic filtering shall preserve its state and authority preconditions. External raw resources shall retain the postconditions of the deliberately selected Abandon operation.

#### 10.2 Storage capabilities and reconstruction

`storage_of(object)` shall return an authorized storage view containing its capacity, alignment, owner, slot identity, and lifetime registration. The view shall remain usable for storage operations while its extent exists, including after the object lifetime ends. The view shall be a borrow with the owner's original authority.

`construct_at<T>(storage, arguments...)` shall require inactive available storage with sufficient capacity, alignment, and a nonoverlapping extent. It shall validate those requirements through its checked storage contract before starting a new T lifetime. T may differ from the prior type. Known violated requirements shall fail compilation under the mandatory memory rules; unresolved runtime conditions shall use the operation's checked failure interface.

Successful reconstruction shall return a pointer to the new generation and register its actual type and destruction operation with the storage owner. A permitted construction unwind shall roll back completed subobjects and leave the extent with its current owner, with no completed replacement generation. The prior ended generation shall remain ended.

An automatic extent's registration shall be bounded by its lexical storage lifetime. Normal scope exit shall destroy its current live registered generation and release the local extent. Replacement shall update that registration; old typed references shall retain their original generation identity.

An inactive member or element extent may host a replacement while its containing storage exists. The replacement shall retain the slot's cleanup rank and register its actual type. Operations on it shall use its new pointer or registration; the original typed member view shall retain its ended generation. Cleanup may manage that registered replacement. Section 11 shall govern any persistent state representation.

`transfer_storage(source, target_owner)` shall require exclusive storage authority, validate the target, then atomically transfer the capability and live registrations. Failure shall retain the original owner. A subsequent failed reconstruction shall retain the storage with the successfully selected new owner.

An automatic extent shall retain its lexical physical lifetime across permitted ownership operations. Release and transfer shall require owning authority. Concurrent mutation, destruction, Abandon, or transfer of one registration shall satisfy Chapter 13's synchronization requirements.

#### 10.3 Pointer and state consequences

A new generation shall require its newly returned pointer or an explicit operation identifying that generation. Earlier pointers and references shall retain their original generation identity. Known stale access shall fail validation; an explicitly checked view shall reject a generation mismatch. Raw access shall retain the selected memory contract's liveness and authority obligations.

An implementation shall preserve the functional distinctions in Section 3 and the results of explicitly selected checked operations. It may encode them statically or in minimal execution state. Additional lifetime-validation tracking shall follow the selected validation mode independently of those functional distinctions.

### 11. ABI Compatibility Constraints

The selected interoperability profile shall determine object-file format, C/C++ symbols, calling conventions, exception boundaries, and class representation.

An extern-compatible class shall preserve the chosen ABI's object fields, base offsets, and virtual representation. Its lifecycle features shall use static resolution, transient out-of-object state, or an explicitly accepted sidecar. A feature requiring persistent state shall obtain a compatible representation before that class can satisfy the requested foreign ABI.

A foreign boundary shall contain Whole through a verified aware contract or an explicit adapter that completes lifecycle coordination and returns compatibly. A CPN26 helper interacting with a foreign destructor shall use that declared continuation contract. Foreign virtual destruction shall require the chosen ABI's representation and dispatch guarantees.

### 12. Required Boundary Examples

| Case | Required behavior |
|---|---|
| A deferred expression reads a constructor parameter modified by an earlier ordinary statement while the frontier is blocked | Read the parameter at the initializer's actual evaluation point. |
| A deferred expression names a constructor-body local | Error; compute the local and use frontier-valid ordinary first assignment instead. |
| A delegated activation would return while its parameter-dependent initializer remains blocked by a later caller assignment | Error: the required producer exceeds its captured parameter lifetime. |
| Two constructor activations explicitly initialize one member | Error even when both expressions produce the same value. |
| An ordinary state obligation is unknown | ANOMALY under the central policy; selected validation adds its check. Functional Pending/Alive routing still selects construction or assignment. |
| Third array-element construction throws with a matching user handler outside construction | Roll back completed elements 1 and 0; never call a destructor for the failed element as a completed object. |
| Numeric Trap occurs in the same expression | Terminate without that rollback or any aggregate traversal. |
| An ordinary destructor body destroys an early base, followed by `log_after()` | Perform the base attempt, then exit through the Whole continuation. |
| Cleanup requests early base destruction, followed by another statement | Do not resume that Cleanup; perform the remaining reverse sweep without reentering it. |
| Automatic earlier member A and manual later member B remain at body exit | Do not destroy A across B; Cleanup and the remainder sweep preserve the B-before-A order. |
| A virtual-base owner transfer is requested inside Cleanup | Reject before changing the owner. |
| An abandoned base layer owned a shared virtual base that was not itself abandoned | Retain the existing frozen claim and discharge it once in the virtual tail. |
| An ordinary caller requests early base destruction of an Alive object | Finish that object's Whole coordination, then resume the external caller through its ordinary call contract. |
| Complete-object Abandon is requested after Destroying begins | Reject: complete-object Abandon requires Alive before destruction entry. |
| Array element 2 is abandoned before reverse array destruction | Destroy remaining live elements in descending order, skipping element 2. |
| A new U construction fails after storage was transferred from owner X to owner Y | Y retains inactive storage; the prior generation remains ended. |
| A source-compatible class feature would require changing an extern-compatible object layout | Reject that interoperability combination or require the explicit compatible sidecar contract. |

---

<a id="chapter-07-numeric-expressions"></a>

## CPN26 Numeric Expressions and Resources Specification

### 1. Integer expression binding

The compiler shall bind integer domains and arithmetic common types using the canonical table in [Chapter 02](#chapter-02-integer-bigint), then test the derived type's availability. The enabled-width set affects materialization, not the derived type. For example, i64 with u64 derives i128 even when i256 is enabled instead; fixed-integer comparisons remain mathematical and require no such widening.

An operation shall retain that selected operand/result type and apply its resolved ordinary policy. An explicit destination on a named arithmetic interface selects that operation's projection type. A surrounding assignment uses the already computed typed value. Narrow integer operands receive exactly the type derived by Chapter 02.

An implicit integer conversion requires whole-domain exact preservation or an exact source value established by language constant evaluation. The compiler shall use those language proofs for binding and overload selection. Optional optimizer analysis may optimize an already bound operation without changing its source type or overload identity. Typed-family unification follows the explicit crossing rules.

### 2. Unary operations and compound assignment

Unary `+` preserves its operand type and value. Unary `~` preserves a fixed integer's type and complements exactly its `N` representation bits. BigInt complement uses the established infinite two's-complement model.

Ordinary unary `-` shall apply the selected integer policy to mathematical negation in the operand type. Native delivers its N-bit modulo interpretation. Checked accepts signed minimum only when its mathematical negation fits the destination; same-type signed minimum therefore fails. Checked unsigned negation accepts zero and reports OutOfRange otherwise. `checked_neg` and `try_neg` select that predicate explicitly; `wrapping_neg` and `saturating_neg` select modulo and clamp projection. Diagnostics follow the central numeric applicability table.

`abs(x)` shall preserve the integer type and apply the selected ordinary policy to its mathematical absolute value. Native therefore maps signed minimum to the same minimum bit pattern; Checked rejects that unrepresentable positive result. `checked_abs` and `try_abs` explicitly select Checked. `magnitude(iN)` returns exact absolute value in enabled `uN`; `magnitude(uN)` is identity. BigInt abs/magnitude retain their exact integer and resource contract.

Prefix and postfix increment/decrement require a writable integer lvalue and use same-type addition/subtraction of one under the resolved ordinary integer policy. Prefix yields the updated lvalue; postfix yields the old value as a value of the operand type. For allocating integers, any snapshot required for postfix must be prepared before mutation; a resource failure leaves the operand unchanged.

For `target op= rhs`, evaluation proceeds as follows:

1. Locate the target once and read its old value.
2. Evaluate `rhs` once.
3. Apply the ordinary operator's type-selection and resolved arithmetic policy.
4. Apply the permitted implicit conversion back to the target type.
5. Commit the write-back on success and yield the target lvalue.

A missing implicit write-back conversion is a type error. It is not a request for implicit truncation or an implicit dynamic narrowing check. Operand side effects are not rolled back. In particular, a right-hand expression's independent mutation is not undone merely because the compound write-back fails.

Explicit `checked_add_assign`, `checked_sub_assign`, `checked_mul_assign`, and `checked_div_assign` instead select the target type as the destination. As ordinary function calls, they evaluate their arguments from left to right; the target argument locates the mutable target, and the function reads its then-current value after argument evaluation. They compute the exact mathematical operation on their admitted integer operands, check that destination, and commit only on success. Their `try_*_assign` counterparts return `NumericResult<void>`; success contains status and no additional value snapshot. The value/Trap forms return `void`. They do not require an otherwise unavailable arithmetic common type because the destination has been selected explicitly. Typed-family restrictions still apply. The compound operator's earlier old-value read is not implicitly transferred to these function calls.

For example, with a runtime `i16 y`, `i8 x; x += y;` requires an implicit write-back proof and is otherwise ill-typed. `try_add_assign(x, y)` explicitly requests checked write-back to `i8`; failure leaves `x` unchanged.

### 3. Numeric tokens, propagation, and materialization

#### 3.1 Lexical forms

Integer tokens use decimal digits or explicit radix prefixes:

```text
decimal:  0, 42, 012
binary:   0b101010
octal:    0o52
hex:      0x2A
```

Prefixes are case-insensitive. Leading zero alone does not select octal: `012` is decimal twelve. A single underscore may separate two digits of the same digit sequence, as in `1_000` or `0xDE_AD`. Separators cannot lead, trail, repeat, or immediately follow a radix prefix. An invalid digit for the selected radix is an error. Integer tokens have no implicit unsigned, long, or host-width suffix. Explicit type construction supplies a type.

The sign is a unary operator, not part of an integer token. Exact literal processing nevertheless precedes fixed-width materialization, so `-2147483648` can bind directly to `i32` without first materializing positive `2147483648` as `i32`.

Decimal real tokens have either a decimal point with digits on both sides, an exponent, or both: `0.5`, `1e3`, `1.25e-4`. A hexadecimal real token has a `0x` prefix and mandatory binary exponent introduced by `p`, for example `0x1p0` or `0x1.8p+2`. Its optional point also has digits on both sides. Exponent signs are optional and exponent digits are decimal. The same separator restrictions apply independently to each digit sequence. NaN and infinity are representation values, not numeric-token spellings.

Real tokens denote exact rational mathematical values before materialization. A negative real zero retains its requested sign. No token is parsed through the compiler host's floating format.

Neither integer nor real tokens carry legacy type suffixes. `Type name(exact_literal);` or an explicit numeric construction/cast supplies the destination; additional suffix families are not required.

#### 3.2 Untyped integer expressions

An integer token initially has an abstract compile-time integer value. Parentheses, unary `+`/`-`, and literal-only `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` preserve that abstract category. Division truncates toward zero; `%` uses the corresponding dividend-signed remainder. The compiler does not insert fixed-width overflow into this abstract calculation.

An abstract integer expression materializes when a concrete numeric type is required: an explicit construction, binding to a typed arithmetic operand, a declared numeric destination, a parameter type, or default value inference. Default unconstrained materialization uses the resolved default integer type, as selected by Chapter 08. Failure to fit that type is `ERROR`; there is no automatic unsigned, wider-integer, or BigInt fallback.

For an ordinary arithmetic operation with one typed integer operand and one abstract integer operand, the abstract value binds to that operand's type and must fit it. A surrounding destination cannot change this binding. Both operands then follow the ordinary typed rules. An explicit type on the other operand can instead request a different common type.

Comparison may compare an abstract integer directly with an admitted typed integer's mathematical value without materializing the constant into that type. For example, `u8(255) < 300` is true. An all-abstract comparison returns a Boolean without materializing its operands as runtime integers.

Width-dependent operations—`~`, `&`, `|`, `^`, and shifts—materialize their participating integer values before operating. The type comes from an explicit width-bearing operation, an admitted typed operand, or the direct numeric destination when all relevant operands remain untyped; otherwise it is the default integer type. Shift counts retain their mathematical input value; the selected operation policy determines count validation or Native mapping.

Named numeric conversion functions consume an abstract literal's exact value directly. They do not first materialize it in the destination. Therefore `wrapping_cast<u8>(-1)` yields `255`; `try_checked_cast<u8>(-1)` returns `Err(OutOfRange)`; ordinary direct literal binding `u8(-1)` is a materialization error.

#### 3.3 Floating and exact-family boundaries

An abstract numeric literal directly bound to a fixed floating format rounds to that format, using the resolved compile-time literal-rounding policy, as selected by Chapter 08. An unconstrained real token shall use the floating literal default in Chapter 08. Literal formation produces a constant representation; it does not generate an execution-time sticky flag on every use. A finite literal is rejected for target-format Overflow under its selected literal rounding policy. Classification uses the specified precision-rounded unbounded-exponent result; it does not reject every exact source magnitude slightly above `MAX_FINITE` when that source rounds to the finite maximum without Overflow. Inexact or subnormal formation is permitted under the declared policy and applicable diagnostics. Compile-time formation events do not enter runtime sticky status. Named casts retain their own specified predicates and status delivery; Exact still requires exact finite representability.

Floating operators are typed operations. With only untyped operands, their operands first bind to the directly expected floating format, or otherwise to the default floating format; each token is rounded directly to that format. The operation then performs its ordinary floating calculation and status effects. A floating `0.0 / 0.0` remains a floating operation: an observed invocation records Invalid, while an ordinary Native invocation uses its provider result with unobserved events. Mandatory constant evaluation uses its separate target-semantic rule.

An already typed operand or subexpression remains a rounding boundary. `f64(0.1)` converted to Rational uses that encoded `f64`; direct construction of Rational from token `0.1` uses the exact rational token value. Exact-family arithmetic requires the established explicit operand binding; an existing typed floating operation shall retain its selected floating contract across destination binding.

Explicit casts use their own rounding or exactness predicates and report their own status. In particular, `try_exact_cast<f32>(0.1)` probes the exact token value; it does not probe an already rounded `f32` constant.

#### 3.4 Named special-value construction
